title: The Pale
hookLine: the Russian Empire confines most Jews to its western provinces

lines: A LINE WRITTEN IN A LAW.
ON THE OTHER SIDE, THE ROAD ENDS.
cards: A Jewish trader has goods to sell in a city a few days' ride to the east. The roads are open, the horse is ready, the buyers are waiting. And he cannot simply go.
No wall stands in his way, no river. The line he cannot cross is written in a law, drawn on a map in an office far away. On one side, he may live, trade, marry and be buried.
On the other, for him, the road ends, unless an official grants a permit he may never get. His Christian neighbor can take that road tomorrow. Today, a boundary with a name: the Pale.

teach.b: When the Russian Empire took over lands that had belonged to Poland, it took over their Jewish communities too, the world of the Council of Four Lands, the Baal Shem Tov and the Vilna Gaon.
The empire's answer was a boundary. Jews were, with some exceptions, allowed to live only in its western provinces, and kept out of the Russian heartland and its great cities.
That region came to be called the Pale of Settlement. Inside it, life was crowded and often poor, but also full: market towns, study houses, Hasidic courts, the yeshiva at Volozhin.
A whole Yiddish-speaking world grew up inside a line someone else had drawn. In Hebrew and Yiddish the Pale had its own name, techum ha-moshav, the boundary of settlement.
And techum, boundary, already meant something in Jewish life: the limit on how far a person walks on Shabbat. It goes back to a verse about the manna in the wilderness.

In the JPS translation of Exodus, the Israelites are told: "abide ye every man in his place, let no man go out of his place on the seventh day." The rabbis read that as a measured distance around a town.
So Jews in the Pale knew two boundaries by the same name.

One was chosen, taken on as holy rest, and lifted every week when Shabbat ended. The other was imposed by a government that did not want them, and did not lift at sunset. One limit was a gift you kept.
The other was a fence kept around you.

how: Jews who keep Shabbat by traditional law observe the techum, staying within a set walking distance of the town where they spend the day.

o: the line around a city's walled Jewish quarter
the region where Russia's Jews were required to live
a stone wall the tsar built along the border

p: western provinces where Jews had to live
a walking limit taken on as rest
let no man go out of his place

s: the Pale was a physical wall around Jewish towns
it was a line in law, drawn on a map, not a wall.
inside the Pale there were yeshivas, Hasidic courts and market towns
a whole Yiddish-speaking world grew up inside the line.
techum is also the word for the Shabbat walking limit
the rabbis drew it from Exodus 16:29.

games.q: you're a Jewish trader at the edge of the Pale, with buyers waiting in a city beyond it. what does the law allow?
o: ride on, like your Christian neighbor.
stay inside the line, unless you belong to an exception the law allows.
move your whole family east for good.
games.why: Jews were, with some exceptions, required to live inside the Pale, and kept out of the Russian heartland.

practice: Think of where your feet can take you without asking anyone's permission, a store, a friend's street, another town, and let one place come clearly to mind.
Then, gently, remember the trader at the edge of the Pale, horse ready and nowhere to ride, and hold both pictures.

wordCard.voice: The Pale. The Pale of Settlement, the western provinces of the Russian Empire where Jews were, with some exceptions, required to live. In Hebrew, techum ha-moshav. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: boundary. The Pale was techum ha-moshav; the Shabbat walking limit is techum Shabbat.

carryVoice: Your line: a fence kept around you. Not every boundary is a gift. See you tomorrow.
